about.heading: Improving care for severe mental illness, locally and globally.
paragraphs: Dr. Rick Wolthusen is a psychiatrist in the Division of Psychotic Disorders at McLean Hospital and an Instructor in Psychiatry at Harvard Medical School. His clinical work focuses on people living with psychosis, bipolar disorder, and catatonia — including complex, recurrent forms of catatonia that may require longer-term management.

His research grows directly out of clinical practice. He has published on catatonia across a range of settings, including low-resource environments and different linguistic and cultural contexts, and serves on the Medical Advisory Board of the Catatonia Foundation. He is also Head of Training and Education for the Chester M. Pierce Division of Global Psychiatry at Massachusetts General Hospital.

A central theme of his work is strengthening the connection between specialist psychiatric care and the communities in which patients live — partnering with patients, families, community health workers, and religious and community leaders to improve recognition of severe mental illness, reduce stigma, and support sustained engagement with care. This work spans Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Ecuador, South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand.

A growing part of his work is bringing lessons from global mental health back to the United States: adapting community- and culturally informed approaches to inpatient psychiatry, and training clinicians, chaplains, and other members of care teams to better recognise severe mental illness, suicide risk, and the cultural contexts that shape psychiatric care.

publications.heading: Contributions to science.
publications.note: Click any title to preview a summary — click it again to open the full publication.

items.title: A Two-Stage Allostatic Model of Catatonia: From Severity Marker to Sensitized Vulnerability
items.authors: Wolthusen RPF, Valcourt SC, England ML, Stoklosa JB • Schizophrenia Research • 2026
items.summary: A new framework reframing catatonia as a condition that can recur and sensitise over time — with direct implications for how clinicians treat, taper, and monitor it.

items.title: Diagnosing and Treating Catatonia in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Scoping Review
items.authors: Belz F, … Wolthusen RPF • Comprehensive Psychiatry • 2025
items.summary: A scoping review of how catatonia is recognised and treated where psychiatric resources are scarce — and what high-income systems can learn in return.

items.title: Design Thinking for Cross-Sector Collaboration in Mental Health: The Brain Spirit Desk Model
items.authors: Wolthusen RPF, Kumado JA, Adomdza GK • Psychiatric Services • 2025
items.summary: How a collaborative 'desk' in Ghana brings mental health professionals together with religious and community leaders — increasing screening, referral, and trust.

items.title: Financing Community Mental Health Worker Programs in the United States: Three Paths Forward
items.authors: Meyerson J, Shepard M, Wolthusen RPF • Community Mental Health Journal • 2026
items.summary: Three practical financing pathways for sustaining community mental health worker programmes — a workforce model drawn from global mental health practice.

items.title: A Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education: Could I, Would I, Should I?
items.authors: Wolthusen RPF, El-Tohami M, Hendler RA, Riordan PA, Stoklosa JB • Academic Psychiatry • 2024
items.summary: A practical framework helping educators and trainees decide when artificial intelligence genuinely adds value to psychiatric training — and when it does not.

items.title: Applying a Socioecological Model Lens to Improve Equity and Inclusion in Global Mental Health Conferences
items.authors: Wolthusen RPF, Read U, Kpobi L, et al. • World Cultural Psychiatry Research Review • 2025
items.summary: A practical analysis of who gets to speak, lead, and be heard at global mental health conferences — and how to make the field measurably more inclusive.

items.title: Reflections From Ghana on Psychiatry, Community, and Mutual Growth
items.summary: A first-person reflection on how community connection and mutual learning shape meaningful psychiatric practice across cultures — and what the Global North can learn in return.

items.title: Cortical Brain Abnormalities in 4,474 Individuals With Schizophrenia (ENIGMA Consortium)
items.authors: van Erp TGM, … Wolthusen RPF, et al. • Biological Psychiatry • 2018 • 1,100+ citations
items.summary: A landmark ENIGMA Consortium mega-analysis mapping cortical thickness and surface area abnormalities across nearly 4,500 individuals with schizophrenia.
